lessons.title: Current, potential difference, resistance and Ohm's law

objectives: Define current, potential difference and resistance with their units.
State and use Ohm's law V = IR and the graph of V against I.
Combine resistors in series and in parallel.
reviewNotes: Units written as A, V, Ω; formulae V = IR, Q = It standard. Check the syllabus for resistivity (ρ = RA/L), which is not included here.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Current, p.d. and resistance
blocks.md: **Current I = Q ÷ t** (charge per second): unit **ampere (A)** = 1 C/s, measured with an **ammeter in series**. **Potential difference (p.d.) V** is the energy transferred per coulomb: unit **volt (V)** = 1 J/C, measured with a **voltmeter in parallel**. **Resistance R = V ÷ I**, unit **ohm (Ω)**. **Ohm's law**: for a metal at constant temperature, **V = I R**: current is proportional to p.d.

blocks.caption: Measuring current (ammeter in series) and p.d. (voltmeter across the resistor).
blocks.alt: A circuit with a cell, a resistor R and an ammeter in the top wire, an open switch at the bottom and a voltmeter connected across the resistor.

blocks.caption: V-I graph for a 2 Ω resistor: a straight line through the origin.
blocks.alt: A graph of V against I: a straight line from the origin through the point 2 A, 4 V; its gradient is the resistance, 2 ohms.

blocks.title: Series and parallel
blocks.md: **Series**: same current everywhere; p.d.s add up to the supply; **R = R₁ + R₂**. **Parallel**: same p.d. across each branch; branch currents add; **1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂** (the total is less than the smallest resistor). The resistance of a wire **increases with length**, **decreases with cross-sectional area**, and depends on the material; for a metal it rises with temperature.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- An ammeter has very low resistance and goes in **series**; a voltmeter has very high resistance and goes in **parallel**.
- In parallel use 1/R, then invert the answer.
- The V-I graph of a filament lamp is a curve: it does not obey Ohm's law because its temperature rises.

blocks.title: Ohm's law
blocks.statement: A p.d. of 12 V is applied across a 4 Ω resistor. Find the current.

blocks.title: Two resistors
blocks.statement: A 6 Ω and a 3 Ω resistor are connected to a 12 V supply. Find the total resistance and the current when they are (a) in series and (b) in parallel.
blocks.answer: Series 9 Ω, 1.33 A; parallel 2 Ω, 6 A

lessons.title: Electrical power, energy and domestic electricity
lessons.programRef: Form 4 Physics — Current, p.d., resistance, Ohm's law, power and domestic electricity (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)

objectives: Calculate electrical power P = VI and energy E = Pt.
Calculate the energy in kWh and its cost.
Describe fuses, earthing and safe use of mains electricity.
reviewNotes: Mains voltage (220 V) and the price of electricity are assumed values; the tariff is illustrative and must not be taken as the real price.
Fuse sizes (5, 10, 13 A) follow a common school example; check the standard in use locally.
Safety advice general, to be reviewed by a qualified electrician.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Power and energy
blocks.md: **Electrical power P = V × I**, also **P = I² R = V² ÷ R**; unit the **watt (W)**. **Energy E = P × t**: in joules if P is in W and t in s. The household unit is the **kilowatt-hour (kWh)**: **1 kWh = 1 kW × 1 h = 3.6 × 10⁶ J**. **Cost = number of kWh × price per kWh**. The mains in Cameroon is about 220 V a.c. (alternating current, 50 Hz).

blocks.caption: A mains circuit: the fuse and switch are in the live wire.
blocks.alt: A circuit with a source on the left, a fuse and a switch in the top (live) wire, a lamp on the right and the neutral wire along the bottom.

blocks.title: Fuses, earthing and safety
blocks.md: A **fuse** is a thin wire that **melts** and breaks the circuit if the current is too large; it goes in the **live** wire with a rating **just above** the normal current. The **earth wire** joins the metal case of an appliance to the ground so that a fault current flows to earth and blows the fuse instead of shocking you. **Switches** go in the live wire. A **circuit breaker** does the same job as a fuse and can be reset.

blocks.title: Safety at home
blocks.md: Do not touch switches, plugs or wires with wet hands; do not overload sockets with many appliances; replace damaged cables; never push objects into sockets; keep children away; switch off before repairs; and let a **qualified electrician** do any mains wiring. Wire colour codes vary between wiring systems: always follow the local code.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Convert to kW and hours for kWh: 1500 W for 2 h = 1.5 kW × 2 h = 3 kWh, not 3000.
- A fuse protects the **wiring** from overheating; it does not make an appliance safe by itself.
- A fuse in the neutral wire would leave the appliance live when it blows.

blocks.title: Current and fuse
blocks.statement: A 2200 W heater runs on 220 V. Find the current and suggest a suitable fuse from 5 A, 10 A and 13 A.
steps: A 10 A fuse would be at the limit; a 13 A fuse is just above the normal current.
